question: What are the most common Spring Security interview questions for freshers?
title: Top Spring Security Interview Questions — Fresher Preparation Guide
direct_answer: Top Spring Security questions for freshers cover authentication vs authorization, filter chain flow, UserDetailsService, JWT token generation and validation, SecurityFilterChain configuration, password encoding with BCrypt, CSRF protection in REST APIs, method-level security with @PreAuthorize, and HTTP status codes 401 vs 403.

interviewer_intent.testing: Breadth of Spring Security knowledge and ability to explain core concepts clearly in a fresher interview context
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Memorizing definitions without practical understanding — unable to explain when to use JWT vs session or why CSRF is disabled for stateless APIs
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Demonstrate hands-on experience by mentioning specific implementation challenges you solved, like handling token expiry or securing REST endpoints with role-based access

sections.title: Essential Spring Security Topics for Fresher Interviews
sections.content:
Spring Security interviews for freshers focus on **foundational concepts** and **practical implementation patterns** in modern REST APIs. Interviewers want to see you understand the **authentication vs authorization** distinction — authentication proves who you are (login with credentials), authorization decides what you can access (roles and permissions).

You'll be asked about the **filter chain**, which intercepts every HTTP request and applies security checks before it reaches your controller. The **UserDetailsService** is critical — it loads user data from your database during login. For **JWT-based authentication**, you need to explain token generation, validation, and storage. Understanding **SecurityFilterChain** configuration shows you can set up URL-based security rules. **PasswordEncoder** with BCrypt is the standard for hashing passwords securely. You must know why **CSRF protection is disabled** for stateless REST APIs but enabled for server-rendered pages. **Method-level security** with @PreAuthorize adds fine-grained control inside service layers. Finally, distinguishing **401 Unauthorized** (not authenticated) from **403 Forbidden** (authenticated but not authorized) shows attention to detail.

sections.title: Complete Spring Security Configuration Example
When These Questions Appear in Interviews
sections.content: These questions appear in **entry-level backend developer interviews** where Spring Boot REST APIs are part of the job description. Expect them when the role involves building or maintaining **microservices with JWT authentication** or integrating with **OAuth2 providers** like Google or GitHub. Interviewers ask these when they want to assess if you can **independently implement authentication** without copy-pasting tutorials. You'll face deeper dives if the job requires **role-based access control (RBAC)** for multi-tenant systems or **securing internal APIs** in a service mesh. Prepare these topics thoroughly for **product companies** and **startups** where you'll be expected to own security implementation from day one.

sections.title: Common Mistakes Freshers Make
sections.content:
- **Confusing authentication with authorization**: Freshers say "Spring Security does authentication" without explaining that authorization (roles/permissions) is equally important.
- **Not knowing the filter chain order**: They can't explain that JWT filters run before UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter or why custom filters must be placed correctly.
- **Storing plain passwords**: Freshers forget to use PasswordEncoder and store raw passwords in the database, a critical security flaw.
- **Leaving CSRF enabled for REST APIs**: This breaks POST/PUT/DELETE requests with 403 errors because stateless APIs don't need CSRF tokens.
- **Using @PreAuthorize without @EnableMethodSecurity**: The annotation is silently ignored, and they spend hours debugging why method security doesn't work.

sections.title: Key Points to Remember
content: **Authentication**: Verifies user identity through credentials (username/password, JWT token, OAuth2)
**Authorization**: Determines what authenticated users can access based on roles and permissions
**SecurityFilterChain**: Defines URL-based security rules like public endpoints, role requirements, and session policies
**UserDetailsService**: Interface to load user data from database during authentication, returns UserDetails object
**JWT**: Stateless token containing user info and expiry, validated on every request without server-side session storage
**BCryptPasswordEncoder**: One-way hashing algorithm with automatic salt generation, industry standard for password storage
**CSRF Protection**: Cross-Site Request Forgery prevention, disabled for stateless REST APIs, enabled for form-based apps
**@PreAuthorize**: Method-level security annotation that checks expressions like hasRole before method execution
**401 vs 403**: 401 means unauthenticated (no valid token), 403 means authenticated but insufficient permissions

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The most common Spring Security questions for freshers cover core concepts and practical implementation. First, you need to understand authentication versus authorization — authentication is proving who you are with credentials or tokens, while authorization decides what resources you can access based on roles. Interviewers always ask about the filter chain because that's how Spring Security intercepts requests before they reach your controller. You'll need to explain UserDetailsService, which loads user data from your database during login, and how it returns a UserDetails object with username, password, and authorities. JWT questions are standard — how do you generate a token with user info and expiry, how do you validate it on every request, and where do you store it on the client side. SecurityFilterChain configuration comes up because that's where you define which URLs are public, which need authentication, and which require specific roles like ADMIN. Password encoding is critical — you must use BCryptPasswordEncoder to hash passwords, never store them plain. For REST APIs, you'll be asked why CSRF is disabled — it's because stateless APIs don't use cookies or sessions, so CSRF attacks aren't relevant. Method-level security with at-PreAuthorize lets you add checks inside service methods, like at-PreAuthorize hasRole ADMIN on deleteUser. Finally, know the difference between 401 and 403 status codes — 401 means you're not logged in at all, 403 means you're logged in but don't have permission. One mistake freshers make is not connecting these concepts to real code. When I explain JWT, I mention storing the token in localStorage on the frontend and sending it in the Authorization header with Bearer prefix. That shows I've actually implemented it, not just read about it. Another pitfall is forgetting that at-PreAuthorize needs at-EnableMethodSecurity to work — without that annotation, your security checks are silently ignored and you'll debug for hours.

question: What is the difference between Spring Security's @EnableWebSecurity and @EnableMethodSecurity?
title: @EnableWebSecurity vs @EnableMethodSecurity in Spring Security
direct_answer: @EnableWebSecurity activates Spring Security's web-layer security, including the filter chain and URL-based access control through SecurityFilterChain. @EnableMethodSecurity enables method-level security annotations like @PreAuthorize, @PostAuthorize, and @Secured on service methods. Both annotations serve different layers and are typically used together in production applications.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding that Spring Security operates at two layers — web/filter layer and method/service layer — and requires separate activation
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Adding @PreAuthorize on service methods without @EnableMethodSecurity, causing security checks to be silently ignored with no error or warning
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that @EnableMethodSecurity replaced the deprecated @EnableGlobalMethodSecurity in Spring Security 6.0 and supports SpEL expressions more cleanly

sections.title: Two Layers of Spring Security Activation
sections.content:
Spring Security operates at **two distinct layers** in your application, and each requires its own activation annotation. **@EnableWebSecurity** turns on the **web security layer** — this includes the filter chain that intercepts HTTP requests, URL pattern matching with requestMatchers, and SecurityFilterChain bean configuration.

Think of it as the **gatekeeper at the door** checking if requests can even reach your application. **@EnableMethodSecurity** activates the **method security layer** — this enables annotations like @PreAuthorize, @PostAuthorize, and @Secured that you place directly on service or controller methods. It's like having **individual room locks** inside the building where each method checks its own access rules. Most production applications use **both annotations together** because they complement each other — web security handles broad URL-based rules (all admin endpoints need authentication), while method security adds fine-grained control (only users with MANAGER role can approve invoices). Without @EnableWebSecurity, Spring Security doesn't start at all. Without @EnableMethodSecurity, your @PreAuthorize annotations are **silently ignored** with no error, which is a common source of security bugs.

sections.title: @EnableWebSecurity vs @EnableMethodSecurity
sections.content:
blue|@EnableWebSecurity|~URL-level security|Activates the filter chain|Secures endpoints by path|SecurityFilterChain bean
emerald|@EnableMethodSecurity|~method-level security|Enables @PreAuthorize / @PostAuthorize|Secures service methods|SpEL on roles + arguments
amber|Together|~defense in depth|URL rules as the first gate|Method checks closest to the data

sections.title: Key Differences Between the Two Annotations

rows: On same or separate configuration class

sections.title: Both Annotations Working Together
When to Use Each Annotation
sections.content:
Use **@EnableWebSecurity** when you need to configure Spring Security at the web layer — this is **always required** in any Spring Boot application using Spring Security, even if you don't create a custom SecurityFilterChain (Spring Boot provides defaults).

Apply it on your main security configuration class where you define which URLs are public, which need authentication, and how JWT or session management works.

Use **@EnableMethodSecurity** when you need **method-level authorization checks** beyond simple URL patterns. For example, if your /api/orders endpoint should be accessible to authenticated users, but only users with MANAGER role can call orderService.cancelOrder(), you need method security. It's essential when **business logic requires role checks** that can't be expressed as URL patterns, like "users can view their own profile but admins can view anyone's profile". In practice, **use both annotations together** — @EnableWebSecurity handles the outer perimeter (authentication, public endpoints), and @EnableMethodSecurity adds inner defenses (role-specific method access).

sections.title: Common Mistakes Freshers Make
sections.content:
- **Adding @PreAuthorize without @EnableMethodSecurity**: This is the most common mistake — freshers annotate methods with @PreAuthorize but forget to enable method security, so the annotations are completely ignored without any error message. Spring silently skips the security check, leaving methods unprotected.
- **Using only @EnableWebSecurity and expecting method security to work**: Freshers think one annotation enables everything, then wonder why their @PreAuthorize checks don't trigger.
- **Not knowing @EnableMethodSecurity replaced @EnableGlobalMethodSecurity**: In Spring Security 6, the old annotation was deprecated, and code using it throws warnings. Freshers copying old tutorials get confused.
- **Placing @EnableMethodSecurity on the wrong class**: It must be on a Spring configuration class (with @Configuration) to be processed — putting it on a service class does nothing.

sections.title: Key Points to Remember
content: **@EnableWebSecurity**: Activates Spring Security's filter chain and web-layer security, required for any Spring Security setup
**@EnableMethodSecurity**: Enables method-level security annotations like @PreAuthorize, @PostAuthorize, @Secured on service methods
**Two Layers**: Web security handles HTTP request filtering and URL patterns, method security handles business logic authorization
**Silent Failure**: Without @EnableMethodSecurity, @PreAuthorize annotations are ignored with no error, creating security vulnerabilities
**Typical Usage**: Both annotations are used together on the main security configuration class for complete coverage
**Spring Security 6**: @EnableMethodSecurity replaced the deprecated @EnableGlobalMethodSecurity with cleaner SpEL support
**Placement**: Both annotations must be on a @Configuration class to be processed by Spring container
**SecurityFilterChain vs Annotations**: @EnableWebSecurity uses SecurityFilterChain beans, @EnableMethodSecurity uses annotations directly on methods

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The difference between at-EnableWebSecurity and at-EnableMethodSecurity is about which layer of security they activate. at-EnableWebSecurity turns on Spring Security's web layer — that's the filter chain that intercepts HTTP requests before they reach your controller. It's where you configure SecurityFilterChain to define which URLs are public, which need authentication, and which require specific roles. For example, you'd use it to say all endpoints under slash-api slash-admin need ADMIN role. Without this annotation, Spring Security doesn't start at all, and your app has no security. at-EnableMethodSecurity is for the method layer — it activates annotations like at-PreAuthorize and at-PostAuthorize that you put directly on service methods. This is for fine-grained authorization inside your business logic. For instance, if you have a method like approveInvoice, you can add at-PreAuthorize hasRole MANAGER to ensure only managers can call it, even if the URL is accessible to all authenticated users. The key thing is these two annotations work at different levels and you typically need both. Web security is the outer gate checking requests, method security is the inner locks on individual operations. One common mistake freshers make is adding at-PreAuthorize on methods but forgetting to add at-EnableMethodSecurity to the configuration class. When that happens, Spring silently ignores your at-PreAuthorize annotations — there's no error, no warning, the method just runs without any security check. That's a serious vulnerability. Another thing to know is that at-EnableMethodSecurity replaced the old at-EnableGlobalMethodSecurity in Spring Security 6. If you see code with the old annotation, it's deprecated and you should use the new one. In my own projects, I always put both annotations on the same security configuration class. at-EnableWebSecurity handles the filter chain setup, and at-EnableMethodSecurity enables method annotations. That way, I have complete security coverage — broad URL rules at the web layer and specific role checks at the method layer.

beats.content: @EnableWebSecurity activates Spring Security's filter-based web security — the SecurityFilterChain bean, URL authorization rules, filter chain registration. In Spring Boot it's technically optional because security auto-configuration handles it, but it's standard practice to include it explicitly.

@EnableMethodSecurity activates AOP-based method security — it's what makes @PreAuthorize, @PostAuthorize, and @Secured work. This is NOT auto-configured in Spring Boot. Without it, those annotations are silently ignored. No error, no warning, just no security.

question: How would you explain how Spring Security works to an interviewer?
title: How Spring Security Works — Complete Explanation for Interviews
direct_answer: Spring Security works through a filter chain that intercepts every HTTP request before it reaches your controllers. The filters handle: loading the SecurityContext, authenticating credentials, checking authorization, and handling exceptions. The SecurityContext stores the current user's Authentication throughout the request.

interviewer_intent.testing: High-level architectural understanding — the most common Spring Security interview question
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Only describing annotations without explaining the underlying filter chain
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a structured answer: filter chain → SecurityContext → Authentication object → authorization check

sections.title: Spring Security Architecture: Filter Chain and SecurityContext
sections.content:
Spring Security protects your application by inserting a **filter chain** between the incoming HTTP request and your controllers.

Think of it like airport security — every passenger (request) must pass through multiple checkpoints (filters) before boarding the plane (reaching your controller). The **SecurityFilterChain** contains 10-15 filters that run in sequence: one loads user credentials, another validates them, another checks permissions, and so on. The critical piece is the **SecurityContext** — a thread-local storage that holds the **Authentication** object representing the currently logged-in user. Once a filter authenticates the user (say, by validating a JWT token or session), it stores the Authentication in the SecurityContext. Later filters and your controller code can access it via SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication(). Without Spring Security, you'd have to manually write all this authentication and authorization logic in every controller method.

sections.title: Spring Security Request Flow
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart LR A[HTTP request] --> B[Filter chain] B --> C[Authentication filter
extract credentials/token] C --> D[AuthenticationManager
verify] D --> E[SecurityContext
holds the principal] E --> F[Authorization
URL + @PreAuthorize rules] F -->|allowed| G[Controller] F -->|denied| H[403 / 401] ```

sections.title: Basic Spring Security Configuration with Filter Chain
When Spring Security Is Essential
sections.content: Use Spring Security when you need **authentication** (who is the user?) or **authorization** (what can they access?) in your Java application. For a REST API serving mobile apps, you'd use JWT tokens with stateless sessions. For a traditional web app with login pages, you'd use form-based authentication with sessions. For microservices talking to each other, you'd use OAuth2 resource server mode. Even simple CRUD apps need Spring Security to prevent unauthorized data access — without it, anyone can call DELETE /api/users/123 and delete any user. Spring Security also protects against common attacks: CSRF (cross-site request forgery), session fixation, and clickjacking. If your app has users and data worth protecting, Spring Security is the industry-standard solution.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Explaining only annotations**: Freshers say "just add at-PreAuthorize" without understanding the filter chain underneath. The interviewer wants to hear that filters intercept requests BEFORE controllers, not just annotation magic.
- **Not knowing SecurityContext scope**: The SecurityContext is thread-local — it's only accessible within the same request thread. Async methods or new threads don't inherit it automatically.
- **Disabling CSRF without understanding**: Freshers disable CSRF in REST APIs because "it doesn't work" without knowing that CSRF protection is designed for browser-based apps with cookies, not for stateless JWT APIs.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Filter Chain**: 10-15 filters run before your controller, handling authentication, authorization, CSRF protection, and exception handling in sequence
**SecurityContext**: thread-local storage holding the Authentication object for the current request — access it via SecurityContextHolder.getContext()
**Authentication Object**: contains the user's principal (username), credentials (password), and authorities (roles/permissions) — populated by authentication filters
**UserDetailsService**: Spring Security interface your app implements to load user data from database, LDAP, or other source during authentication
**PasswordEncoder**: encrypts passwords using BCrypt or Argon2 — never store plaintext passwords, Spring Security enforces this by default
**AuthenticationManager**: coordinates multiple authentication providers (database, LDAP, OAuth2) — decides which provider handles each authentication attempt
**SecurityFilterChain Bean**: Java-based configuration replacing XML — defines URL rules, authentication methods, and exception handling for your application

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Spring Security works by inserting a filter chain between the HTTP request and your controller. Every request passes through about 10 to 15 filters in sequence. These filters handle things like loading user credentials, validating passwords, checking permissions, and handling errors. The key concept is the SecurityContext — it's a thread-local storage that holds the Authentication object for the current user. Once a filter authenticates the user, it puts their Authentication into the SecurityContext. Later filters and your controller code can retrieve it using SecurityContextHolder dot getContext dot getAuthentication. For example, if you're using JWT tokens, you'd have a custom filter that runs early in the chain. It extracts the JWT from the Authorization header, validates it, and creates an Authentication object with the user's details and roles. That Authentication goes into the SecurityContext. Then, later filters check if the user has the required roles to access the requested URL. If not, Spring Security throws an AccessDeniedException and returns a 403 response. One common mistake is thinking Spring Security only works through annotations like at-PreAuthorize. Those annotations are just the last layer — the filter chain does the heavy lifting before your controller even runs. Another pitfall is not understanding that the SecurityContext is tied to the current thread. If you spawn a new thread or use async methods, that new thread won't have access to the SecurityContext unless you explicitly copy it. In summary, Spring Security is a filter-based framework. Filters authenticate users, store the Authentication in the SecurityContext, and enforce authorization rules. Your application code just retrieves the current user from the SecurityContext whenever it needs to check permissions or log actions.

seo.metaDescription: Complete explanation of how Spring Security works — filter chain, SecurityContext, authentication flow, authorization, 401 vs 403 for Java fresher interviews.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API with JWT-based authentication
speakable_v2.hook: Spring Security is asked in nearly every Java backend interview — and the candidates who stand out can explain the filter chain architecture, not just the annotations on top of it.

beats.content: Spring Security works at the Servlet filter level. Every HTTP request passes through a chain of filters before it ever reaches your DispatcherServlet or controllers. Security is enforced before your code runs.

The filters have defined responsibilities in order. SecurityContextPersistenceFilter loads any existing authentication from the session. UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter handles form login. For JWT-based APIs, your custom filter validates the JWT and populates the SecurityContext. ExceptionTranslationFilter converts security exceptions to 401 or 403 HTTP responses. The final AuthorizationFilter checks whether the current user's roles allow access to the requested URL.

When authentication succeeds — whether through form login or JWT — Spring creates an Authentication object with the user's identity and roles and stores it in a thread-local SecurityContext. Any code in that request can read the current user from there.
You configure all of this through a SecurityFilterChain bean. URL access rules, which auth mechanisms are active, CSRF settings, session management — all defined there.

speakable_v2.cap: Filter chain runs before controllers. Authentication sets the SecurityContext. Authorization checks the SecurityContext against URL rules. That's the full architectural loop.
followup_handoff: The SecurityContext's thread-local storage and lifecycle is a natural follow-up question.
We can also go deeper on how to secure REST APIs specifically — which filters to customize and which to disable.

question: How do you secure REST APIs using Spring Security?
title: Securing REST APIs with Spring Security — JWT Best Practices
direct_answer: Secure REST APIs with: stateless SecurityFilterChain (STATELESS session, CSRF disabled), JWT authentication (custom filter validates JWT per request), URL-based rules (requestMatchers), and optionally method-level security (at-PreAuthorize) for fine-grained data access control.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using form login for REST APIs — wrong approach, returns redirect HTML responses instead of JSON
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a complete answer: stateless + JWT + URL rules + method security + PasswordEncoder + exception handling

sections.title: REST API Security with Stateless JWT Authentication
sections.content:
Securing REST APIs differs fundamentally from traditional web apps. REST APIs are **stateless** — each request contains all authentication data (usually a JWT token), and the server creates no session.

Your Spring Security config must: (1) disable CSRF protection (not needed for stateless APIs), (2) set session policy to STATELESS (no JSESSIONID cookies), (3) add a custom **JWT filter** that runs before authentication filters to extract and validate the JWT, (4) define URL-based authorization rules using requestMatchers, and (5) configure custom exception handlers to return JSON error responses (401/403) instead of HTML redirects. The JWT filter does the heavy lifting: it extracts the token from the Authorization header ("Bearer eyJhbGciOi..."), validates the signature, extracts claims (userId, roles), and creates an **Authentication** object that populates the SecurityContext. Every subsequent request repeats this process — no session means no server-side state.

sections.title: JWT-Secured REST Request
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart LR A[Client login] --> B[Server issues JWT
signed token] B --> C[Client stores token] C --> D[Request + Authorization: Bearer] D --> E[JWT filter
validate signature + expiry] E -->|valid| F[Set SecurityContext
STATELESS] F --> G[Controller] E -->|invalid| H[401 Unauthorized] ```

sections.title: Complete REST API Security Configuration with JWT
When to Use Stateless REST Security
sections.content: Use stateless JWT-based Spring Security for any **REST API** consumed by non-browser clients: mobile apps (iOS/Android), single-page apps (React/Angular making fetch calls), microservices communicating with each other, or third-party integrations. The key indicator is that the client sends an Authorization header with every request — no cookies, no sessions. For example, a React app logs in via POST /api/auth/login, receives a JWT in the response, stores it in localStorage, and includes it in every subsequent API call. The server validates the JWT and rebuilds the Authentication on each request. This scales horizontally because no server holds session state — any server instance can handle any request. Do NOT use this approach for traditional server-rendered web apps (Thymeleaf, JSP) where users log in via HTML forms — those need session-based authentication with cookies.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using formLogin for REST APIs**: Freshers configure formLogin which redirects unauthenticated users to a login page HTML — REST clients expect JSON 401, not an HTML redirect. Use httpBasic or custom JWT filter instead.
- **Forgetting to disable CSRF**: CSRF protection is ON by default. It blocks POST/PUT/DELETE requests unless the client sends a CSRF token — this breaks REST APIs because clients don't have CSRF tokens. Always disable it for stateless APIs.
- **Not configuring exception handlers**: By default, Spring Security redirects to /login on 401 errors — REST clients can't follow redirects. You must implement AuthenticationEntryPoint and AccessDeniedHandler to return JSON responses.
- **Storing JWT in session**: Defeats the purpose of stateless design. The JWT should be stored client-side (localStorage or memory) and sent in the Authorization header, not in a server-side session.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **STATELESS Session Policy**: sessionCreationPolicy set to STATELESS prevents Spring Security from creating JSESSIONID cookies — each request is independent
**CSRF Disabled**: csrf dot disable required for stateless REST APIs because CSRF protection assumes session-based authentication with cookies
**JWT Filter**: custom filter extending OncePerRequestFilter runs before authentication filters to extract JWT from Authorization header and populate SecurityContext
**requestMatchers**: defines URL-based authorization rules — requestMatchers("/api/admin/**") dot hasRole("ADMIN") restricts URLs to specific roles
**Method Security**: at-PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')") on controller methods provides fine-grained authorization checks beyond URL patterns — requires at-EnableMethodSecurity
**PasswordEncoder**: BCryptPasswordEncoder hashes passwords with salt — never store plaintext passwords, Spring Security rejects {noop} passwords in production
**Custom Exception Handlers**: AuthenticationEntryPoint returns JSON 401 for missing/invalid JWT, AccessDeniedHandler returns JSON 403 for insufficient permissions

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: To secure a REST API with Spring Security, you need a stateless configuration because REST APIs don't use sessions. First, set the session creation policy to STATELESS. This tells Spring Security not to create HTTP sessions or JSESSIONID cookies. Second, disable CSRF protection. CSRF is designed for browser-based apps with cookies, but REST APIs use the Authorization header, so CSRF doesn't apply. Third, implement a custom JWT filter. This filter runs before the authentication filters. It extracts the JWT token from the Authorization header, validates the signature, and creates an Authentication object with the user's roles. Then it puts that Authentication into the SecurityContext. This happens on every single request because there's no session to remember the user. Fourth, configure URL-based authorization rules using requestMatchers. For example, you'd allow public access to login and register endpoints, require ADMIN role for admin endpoints, and require authentication for everything else. Fifth, optionally enable method-level security with at-EnableMethodSecurity. This lets you add at-PreAuthorize annotations to controller methods for fine-grained checks, like ensuring users can only access their own data. Sixth, configure custom exception handlers. By default, Spring Security redirects to a login page for 401 errors, but REST clients need JSON responses. Implement AuthenticationEntryPoint to return a JSON 401 response when the JWT is missing or invalid. Implement AccessDeniedHandler to return a JSON 403 response when the user lacks the required role. The biggest mistake freshers make is using formLogin for REST APIs. That configuration redirects to an HTML login page, which breaks mobile apps and JavaScript clients. Another common error is not disabling CSRF — it'll block your POST requests and you'll get cryptic 403 errors. In summary, REST API security is all about stateless JWT authentication. No sessions, no cookies, no CSRF. Just a JWT filter that validates the token on every request and populates the SecurityContext.

beats.content: Start with the SecurityFilterChain configuration. Disable CSRF — JWT in the Authorization header isn't vulnerable to CSRF. Set session management to STATELESS — REST APIs don't use server sessions. Define URL rules: public endpoints like /api/auth/login and /api/auth/register get permitAll, everything else requires authentication.

Add your custom JWT filter with addFilterBefore, positioned before UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter. The filter reads the Authorization Bearer token, validates it with your JwtService, loads the UserDetails, and sets the Authentication in the SecurityContext.

UserDetailsService implementation — loads users from your database

beats.content: non-obvious: Spring Security's default behavior on auth failure is to redirect to /login. That's fine for browsers but breaks REST clients completely. AuthenticationEntryPoint and AccessDeniedHandler override those defaults with proper JSON responses.

speakable_v2.cap: Stateless, CSRF off, JWT filter, JSON error handlers. Those four decisions are what separate a REST-appropriate security config from a browser-oriented one.

question: What is the difference between stateless and stateful Spring Security?
title: Stateless vs Stateful Spring Security — REST vs Web App
direct_answer: Stateful Spring Security stores the Authentication in the HTTP session — the JSESSIONID cookie re-loads it per request. Stateless (STATELESS session policy) creates NO session — the Authentication is rebuilt from the JWT token on every request. REST APIs use stateless; traditional web apps use stateful.

interviewer_intent.testing: Architecture understanding of Spring Security modes
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that stateless requires the SecurityContext to be populated per request by the JWT filter
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that in stateless mode, JWT filter must populate SecurityContext on EVERY request

sections.title: Understanding Stateful vs Stateless Authentication
sections.content:
The stateful vs stateless decision determines WHERE the user's authentication data lives between requests. **Stateful** (Spring Security default) means the server stores the **Authentication** object in the HTTP session after the user logs in. The browser receives a JSESSIONID cookie.

On subsequent requests, Spring Security loads the Authentication from the session using that cookie — the user doesn't re-authenticate. **Stateless** (SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS) means the server creates NO session. Each request must contain full authentication data (typically a JWT token in the Authorization header). The JWT filter extracts the token, validates it, and creates a fresh Authentication object for that request only. After the response, the Authentication is discarded. Traditional web apps (login forms, server-rendered HTML) use stateful mode because browsers automatically send cookies. REST APIs serving mobile apps or SPAs use stateless mode because those clients send the JWT in an Authorization header, not a cookie.

sections.title: Stateless vs Stateful Security
sections.content:
violet|Stateful|~server session|JSESSIONID cookie|Server stores session in memory|Classic server-rendered web apps|Needs CSRF protection
blue|Stateless|~no server session|JWT / token per request|SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS|REST APIs + SPAs/mobile|Scales horizontally
emerald|Pick|~by client|Browser app + session -> stateful|API for SPA/mobile -> stateless

Every request validates JWT and creates Authentication

REST APIs for mobile apps, SPAs, microservices

sections.title: Stateful Default vs Stateless JWT Config
Choosing Between Stateful and Stateless
sections.content:
Use **stateful** Spring Security when you have a traditional web application with server-rendered HTML (Thymeleaf, JSP, Freemarker). Users log in via an HTML form, and the browser automatically sends the JSESSIONID cookie on every request. This is simpler to implement because Spring Security handles session management automatically.

Use **stateless** Spring Security when building REST APIs consumed by non-browser clients: mobile apps (iOS, Android), single-page apps (React, Angular, Vue), or microservices. These clients send a JWT in the Authorization header with every request. Stateless scales better because you don't need sticky sessions — any server instance can validate the JWT. However, you must implement a custom JWT filter to extract and validate the token on every request. Mixed scenario: use stateful for the web admin panel (HTML forms) and stateless for the mobile API (JWT) by configuring multiple SecurityFilterChain beans with different URL patterns.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Not populating SecurityContext in stateless mode**: Freshers configure STATELESS but forget to implement the JWT filter that populates the SecurityContext on every request. Without it, the SecurityContext is empty and all requests are treated as unauthenticated.
- **Using STATELESS but expecting session data**: Setting session policy to STATELESS means HttpSession dot setAttribute won't work for storing user preferences or cart data. You need to store that data client-side or in a database.
- **Mixing cookies and Authorization header**: Trying to use both JSESSIONID cookies and JWT tokens simultaneously creates confusion. Pick one approach per API — cookies for stateful web apps, Authorization header for stateless REST APIs.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Stateful Mode**: default Spring Security behavior — Authentication stored in HTTP session after login, loaded from session on subsequent requests via JSESSIONID cookie
**Stateless Mode**: SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS disables session creation — no JSESSIONID cookie, no server-side state, each request is independent
**JWT Requirement**: stateless mode requires custom filter to extract JWT from Authorization header and populate SecurityContext on EVERY request — no session to cache Authentication
**Session Fixation**: stateful mode is vulnerable to session fixation attacks unless you configure sessionManagement dot sessionFixation dot newSession
**Horizontal Scaling**: stateless mode scales easily because no session state — stateful mode needs sticky sessions or Redis-backed session store for load balancing
**Cookie vs Header**: stateful uses JSESSIONID cookie (browser automatically sends), stateless uses Authorization header (client must explicitly include JWT)
**Logout Handling**: stateful logout invalidates server-side session, stateless logout requires JWT blacklist or short expiration times since server has no state

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Stateful and stateless are two different ways Spring Security handles authentication across multiple requests. Stateful is the default mode. When a user logs in with a username and password, Spring Security creates an Authentication object and stores it in the HTTP session. The browser gets a JSESSIONID cookie. On the next request, Spring Security reads that cookie, looks up the session, and loads the stored Authentication. The user doesn't need to send credentials again. This works great for traditional web apps where users log in via an HTML form and the browser automatically sends cookies. Stateless mode is the opposite. You set the session creation policy to STATELESS in your security config. Now Spring Security doesn't create any session. The client must send authentication data with every single request, usually a JWT token in the Authorization header. You implement a custom JWT filter that runs before the authentication filters. This filter extracts the JWT, validates the signature and expiration, and creates a fresh Authentication object from the token's claims. It puts that Authentication into the SecurityContext. After the response is sent, the SecurityContext is cleared. The next request repeats the entire process. REST APIs use stateless mode because mobile apps and single-page apps send the JWT in an Authorization header, not a cookie. It also scales better — you don't need sticky sessions because any server can validate the JWT. The key difference is where the Authentication lives. In stateful mode, it's in the server's session storage. In stateless mode, it's rebuilt from the JWT on every request. One mistake freshers make is configuring stateless mode but not implementing the JWT filter. Without that filter, the SecurityContext stays empty and all requests are rejected as unauthenticated. Another mistake is trying to use HttpSession dot setAttribute in stateless mode — that won't work because there's no session. In summary, stateful stores Authentication in the session and uses cookies. Stateless rebuilds Authentication from a JWT on every request with no session.

seo.metaTitle: Stateless vs Stateful Spring Security | Java Fresher Interview
seo.metaDescription: Compare stateless and stateful Spring Security — JWT vs session-based, STATELESS policy, SecurityContext lifecycle, horizontal scaling implications.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API with JWT-based authentication
speakable_v2.hook: Stateless and stateful Spring Security look similar to configure but have a completely different lifecycle for the SecurityContext — and the JWT filter's behavior depends entirely on which mode you're in.

beats.content: In stateful mode, after a successful login, Spring stores the Authentication in an HTTP session. Every subsequent request arrives with a JSESSIONID cookie, Spring loads the session, and the SecurityContext is restored with the user's Authentication. The user stays logged in across requests.

In stateless mode with SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS, Spring never creates a session. The SecurityContext starts completely empty on every single request. Your JWT filter is responsible for rebuilding it — it reads the token, validates it, loads the UserDetails, and sets the Authentication. After the request completes, the context is cleared. Next request starts fresh.

sharp edge: in stateless mode, if your JWT filter fails to set the SecurityContext for any reason — expired token, missing header, validation error — the request continues with an empty context and hits the authorization check as unauthenticated. This is correct behavior, but it means your filter must handle all JWT error cases gracefully and return 401 rather than letting the request continue.

speakable_v2.cap: Stateful: session restores the SecurityContext automatically. Stateless: JWT filter rebuilds it from scratch on every request. There is no persistence between requests in stateless mode.
followup_handoff: SessionCreationPolicy has other values besides STATELESS and IF_REQUIRED — ALWAYS and NEVER have specific use cases.
The SecurityContext clearing at end of request is handled by SecurityContextPersistenceFilter — understanding that filter explains the lifecycle.

question: How do you handle Spring Security exceptions in a REST API?
title: Spring Security Exception Handling for REST APIs — 401 and 403 JSON Responses
direct_answer: Implement AuthenticationEntryPoint to return JSON 401 for unauthenticated requests (instead of redirect). Implement AccessDeniedHandler to return JSON 403 for unauthorized requests. Configure them in the SecurityFilterChain with exceptionHandling().

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical REST security — returning proper JSON errors vs HTML redirects
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Spring Security returns HTML redirects for 401/403 by default — REST clients can't handle this
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show both AuthenticationEntryPoint and AccessDeniedHandler implementations

sections.title: Spring Security Exception Handling for REST APIs
sections.content:
By default, Spring Security is designed for browser-based web apps. When an unauthenticated user tries to access a protected resource, Spring Security sends a **redirect** to the login page (HTTP 302). When an authenticated user lacks permissions, it redirects to an access denied page. This behavior breaks REST APIs because mobile apps and JavaScript clients expect JSON responses, not HTML redirects or pages. To fix this, you implement two interfaces: **AuthenticationEntryPoint** (handles authentication failures — missing or invalid JWT) and **AccessDeniedHandler** (handles authorization failures — authenticated but insufficient permissions). These handlers write JSON error responses with appropriate HTTP status codes (401 for unauthenticated, 403 for unauthorized). You register them in your SecurityFilterChain using the exceptionHandling configuration.

This ensures your API returns consistent JSON error format: status code, timestamp, error message, and path. Proper error handling is critical for client-side error display and debugging.

sections.title: 401 vs 403 in Spring Security
sections.content:
amber|401 Unauthorized|~not authenticated|No/invalid credentials or token|Handled by AuthenticationEntryPoint|Tells client: log in first
rose|403 Forbidden|~authenticated, not allowed|Valid login but missing role|Handled by AccessDeniedHandler|Tells client: you can't do this
blue|For REST|~clean JSON errors|Custom entry point + handler|Return JSON body, not a login redirect

sections.title: Custom Exception Handlers for REST API
When Custom Exception Handlers Are Required
sections.content: Use custom exception handlers for ANY REST API secured with Spring Security. The default Spring Security behavior (redirects to /login or /accessDenied) only works for browser-based apps with server-rendered HTML. If your API serves mobile apps, single-page apps, or other services, those clients expect JSON responses with proper HTTP status codes. For example, a React app calling GET /api/admin/users without a JWT should receive a JSON 401 response that the app can display as "Please log in." A mobile app where a regular user tries to DELETE /api/admin/users/123 should receive a JSON 403 response that triggers an "Access denied" alert. Without custom handlers, the client receives HTML redirect responses or error pages, which break JSON parsing and cause cryptic errors. Even for internal microservices, consistent JSON error format helps with centralized logging and monitoring — you can parse the error field to detect authentication vs authorization issues.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Not implementing both handlers**: Freshers implement AuthenticationEntryPoint but forget AccessDeniedHandler, so 403 errors still return HTML. You need BOTH handlers for complete REST error handling.
- **Writing HTML in error response**: Setting the response content type to text/html or forgetting to set it at all — the client expects application/json with a parseable JSON body.
- **Returning generic error messages**: Sending "Access denied" without context. Include the request path and timestamp so clients can log the error details for debugging.
- **Not registering handlers in SecurityFilterChain**: Implementing the handlers but forgetting to configure them with exceptionHandling dot authenticationEntryPoint and exceptionHandling dot accessDeniedHandler — Spring Security still uses the defaults.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **AuthenticationEntryPoint**: handles unauthenticated requests (no JWT, invalid JWT, expired JWT) — returns JSON 401 response instead of redirecting to login page
**AccessDeniedHandler**: handles unauthorized requests (valid JWT but insufficient permissions) — returns JSON 403 response instead of redirecting to access denied page
**Default Behavior**: Spring Security redirects to /login for 401 and /accessDenied for 403 — this breaks REST APIs because clients expect JSON, not HTML
**exceptionHandling Configuration**: register custom handlers in SecurityFilterChain using exceptionHandling dot authenticationEntryPoint and accessDeniedHandler methods
**Consistent Error Format**: return JSON with timestamp, status code, error type, message, and path — matches Spring Boot default error response structure
**ObjectMapper**: use Jackson ObjectMapper to serialize error Map into JSON string — ensures valid JSON format without manual string concatenation
**HttpServletResponse**: set content type to application/json and status code (401 or 403) before writing response body — clients use status code for error handling logic

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Spring Security's default exception handling is designed for browser-based apps, not REST APIs. When an unauthenticated request comes in, Spring Security redirects to the login page. When an authenticated user lacks permissions, it redirects to an access denied page. Those redirects return HTML, which breaks REST clients expecting JSON. To fix this, you implement two custom handlers. First is AuthenticationEntryPoint. This handles authentication failures, like missing JWT or invalid credentials. You implement the commence method. It receives the request, response, and the exception. You set the response content type to application slash json and the status to 401. Then you create a JSON error object with the timestamp, status code, error message, and request path. You use Jackson ObjectMapper to convert that to a JSON string and write it to the response. Second is AccessDeniedHandler. This handles authorization failures, when the user is authenticated but doesn't have the required role. You implement the handle method. Same idea — set content type to JSON, status to 403, create an error map, and write it as JSON. The difference is you use the AccessDeniedException to get the specific permission that was denied. After implementing both handlers, you register them in your SecurityFilterChain. In the exceptionHandling section, you call authenticationEntryPoint with your custom AuthenticationEntryPoint bean and accessDeniedHandler with your custom AccessDeniedHandler bean. Now when a REST client makes a request without a JWT, it gets a clean JSON 401 response saying "Authentication required." When an authenticated user tries to access an admin endpoint without the ADMIN role, they get a JSON 403 response saying "Access denied." The most common mistake is forgetting to implement both handlers. If you only do AuthenticationEntryPoint, you'll still get HTML redirects for 403 errors. Another mistake is not setting the content type to application slash json, so the client tries to parse HTML as JSON and fails. In summary, you need two custom handlers: AuthenticationEntryPoint for 401 errors and AccessDeniedHandler for 403 errors. Both return JSON responses instead of HTML redirects.

seo.metaTitle: Spring Security Exception Handling for REST APIs | Interview
seo.metaDescription: Learn how to handle 401 and 403 as JSON responses in Spring Security REST APIs — AuthenticationEntryPoint, AccessDeniedHandler, exceptionHandling configuration.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API with JWT-based authentication
speakable_v2.hook: By default, Spring Security sends HTML redirects when auth fails — which looks fine in a browser but completely breaks any REST API client expecting JSON.

beats.content: Spring Security has two separate interfaces for the two different failure cases. AuthenticationEntryPoint handles the 401 case — the request has no valid authentication. That includes a missing token, an expired JWT, or an invalid signature. AccessDeniedHandler handles the 403 case — the user is authenticated but their roles don't grant access to the requested resource.

You implement both interfaces by writing directly to the HttpServletResponse: set the content type to JSON, set the appropriate status code, and write a JSON error body. Then you register both in your SecurityFilterChain with the exceptionHandling() DSL.

candidates miss: @ControllerAdvice cannot catch Spring Security exceptions. Those exceptions are thrown in the filter chain — before DispatcherServlet, before your controllers. @ControllerAdvice only handles exceptions that reach the DispatcherServlet. AuthenticationEntryPoint and AccessDeniedHandler are the only way to handle security exceptions with custom responses.

speakable_v2.cap: Implement AuthenticationEntryPoint for 401 JSON, AccessDeniedHandler for 403 JSON, register both in exceptionHandling(). @ControllerAdvice can't do this — security exceptions live in the filter layer.
followup_handoff: CORS headers must be present on 401 responses too — if they're missing, the browser blocks the error response and your frontend sees a CORS error instead of a 401.
We can also look at how to structure a consistent JSON error response DTO for all security errors.
